Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette: Arthur’s seventieth birthday passed without ceremony, but the real turning point arrived nearly a decade earlier, during the sudden, crushing weight of his lungs and the frantic rhythm of the emergency room monitors. He had collapsed at his desk, a familiar headache giving way to a terrifying inability to draw breath. The medical team moved with practiced urgency, tubes finding his throat, cold gel pressing against his chest, the sharp, medicinal scent of antiseptic and crushed linen filling his nostrils. He remembered the drop-ceiling tiles, the fluorescent hum, the feeling that his own chest was a vault sealing shut while strangers in blue scrubs worked to pry it open. He survived, but the recovery did not erase the event; it merely shifted it from a medical crisis to a private siege. Over the months that followed, the sterile odors did not fade. When Arthur sat in his climate-controlled home office, reviewing database schemas on dual monitors, a draft from the ventilation system would carry the faint, ghostly trace of isopropyl and floor wax. Instantly, the memory would surge forward with a clarity that made his ordinary recollections seem dull and half-formed. He would stop typing, certain that the crisis had returned. His heart would hammer against his ribs, and a wave of horror would wash over him, accompanied by a sharp, persistent guilt over the burden his collapse had placed on his ex-wife, and a quiet shame that he had been so helpless. He had come to believe that people could not truly be relied upon, that the systems designed to protect him were fragile, and that the world outside was fundamentally unpredictable and hostile. Arthur stopped sleeping in his bedroom. The house, which should have been his sanctuary, became a landscape of potential hazards. He lay awake, listening to the settling of floorboards, watching the hallway shadows lengthen, convinced that another collapse could begin without warning. His body refused to accept the safety of the present; every minor twinge in his left arm or skip in his pulse was read as a precursor to the dark. He avoided the pharmacy, steering his car past the hospital two blocks from his workplace, and would not enter his quarterly database audit meetings; the sterile, carpeted conference rooms mirrored the trauma space, and Arthur turned his car around instead. At his desk at the corporate office, the environmental control system maintained a precise, climate-controlled chill that mirrored the operating theater. The hum of the HVAC vents and the rhythmic ping of incoming database alerts felt less like professional necessity and more like a countdown. He found himself checking his own smartwatch dozens of times an hour, not out of health consciousness, but to confirm that his body had not yet turned against him. The distance between Arthur’s desk and the world had grown until even a trip to the grocery store left him trembling and exhausted. What finally brought him through the clinic door was a moment of sheer functional breakdown: while trying to reconcile a corrupted backup sequence at 3 a.m., his hands had shaken so violently he could not navigate the mouse, and the sudden realization that he no longer knew how to live without bracing for impact had frightened him more than the illness itself. He sits in the intake room now, his shoulders tight, his eyes fixed on the exit. He does not know if he can ever trust his own physiology again, or the world enough to let it surprise him, but he hopes the silence in his head might finally be replaced by something else.
